# Working governance end to end with the operator paths

In this tutorial you will follow one concern all the way through the governance record — from a colleague voicing a vague frustration to a recorded consent response on a proposal — using the six operator paths in sequence.

You will learn what each path is for, how they hand work to one another by id, and where the confirmation prompts appear. By the end you will have taken a concern to a picture of the governance around it, checked whether the change was yours to make, captured a tension, drafted a proposal, advanced it into circulation, and reviewed and answered a proposal as a responder.

## Prerequisites

- The operating-surface plugin installed. If you have not done that yet, follow [how to install the operating surface](how-to-install-the-operating-surface.md) first.
- A working `glassfrog` install with a stored token. See [how to store a token](../authentication/how-to-store-a-token.md).
- An organization whose plan includes Premium async proposals — the proposal steps need it.
- A Glassfrog organization you are willing to write a real tension and a real draft proposal into. Everything here touches the live record.

Throughout, you talk to your agent in plain language. The paths have **no commands, flags, or arguments of their own** — each is a skill that loads when your need matches it, and delegates to a subagent that does the reading.

---

## Step 1 — Start from a concern and see the governance around it

Begin the way real work begins: with something someone said, and no id in hand.

Tell your agent:

> "Someone on the platform team says onboarding new clinicians keeps stalling on account provisioning. What governance touches this?"

The `governance-navigation` skill loads, and hands the concern to the `governance-navigator` subagent. That subagent searches the record, resolves the roles it matched, finds who fills them, and pulls in the domains and policies that bear on the concern — all in its own context.

What comes back is a **synthesized picture**, not a pile of command output:

- the relevant **roles**, each with a `role_…` id and a one-line note on why it is relevant
- the **fillers** of each role, with `per_` or `agt_` ids
- the governing **domains** and **policies**, each with its id and the role that holds it
- any **notes** — for instance that the picture was narrowed

Notice two things. First, every element carries the id that reads it again, so you can always drop back to the CLI:

```console
$ glassfrog roles role_0123
```

Second, the raw `search` and `roles` output never entered your context. That isolation is the point of delegating.

If the notes say the picture was narrowed, your concern was too broad. Name the circle or the activity and ask again.

---

## Step 2 — Ask whether the change is yours to make

You can now see that account provisioning sits in a domain somewhere. Before doing anything, find out whether you may act.

> "Can I change how clinician accounts get provisioned?"

This is a different question, and a different path — `constraint-discovery` loads instead. If your action is too vague to search for, the **skill itself** asks you to sharpen it before any reading happens. That prompt comes from the skill, not the subagent, because a subagent runs isolated and cannot ask you anything.

Sharpen it and the `constraint-navigator` traverses: search, the roles that matched, their domains and policies, and `me roles` to tell your own roles from someone else's.

The answer comes back as a **characterization composed of three findings**, not one label:

1. **The domain finding** — the governing domain is held by a role you fill, held by another role (named, with its id), or no domain in the record governs it.
2. **Any policies** that shape the action — surfaced *even when the action is inside your own domain*.
3. **Whether this is a change to governance structure**, which goes through a proposal by default.

Two habits to build now, because they are easy to get wrong:

- **"No domain governs it" is not permission.** The absence is reported as an absence. It is not a green light.
- **`owned_by_caller` has three values, not two.** It can be `true`, `false`, or **uncertain** — uncertain whenever the `me roles` list came back incomplete, because `me roles` does not paginate. A role you actually fill is never reported as a confident `false`.

Suppose the picture says the domain belongs to another role, and that the change is structural. That means a proposal — which is where the next four steps go.

---

## Step 3 — Capture the tension

You have a real gap and you know it needs a governance change. Record it.

> "Capture that as a tension on role_0456: the platform circle keeps absorbing provisioning delays it doesn't own."

The `tension-processing` skill delegates to the `tension-processor`. Before it writes anything, it **situates** — reading the tensions already on the role and the ones rolled up from its sub-roles, paging through in full, so the capture is a deliberate addition rather than a blind one.

If your tension matches one already there, you get that existing tension back with `action: surfaced-existing` and **nothing is written**. Refine that one instead.

Otherwise it captures, and you get a record:

- **tension** — `id` (`ten_…`), `sensing_role_id`, `body`, `status`
- **situating** — what it was weighed against
- **action** — `captured`
- **handoff** — the `ten_` id, once the tension is ready to become a governance change

Something you should notice here: **no confirmation prompt appeared.** Tension writes are operational edits, not governance writes, so they are ungated by design. Watch what changes in the next step.

Confirm the record yourself:

```console
$ glassfrog tension get ten_0123
```

---

## Step 4 — Draft the proposal, and meet the gate

Take the `ten_` id forward.

> "Tension ten_0123 is ready. Draft a proposal moving the provisioning accountability to the identity circle's onboarding role."

`proposal-drafting` delegates to the `proposal-drafter`, which grounds the draft in the anchor tension, then situates against the drafts already in flight in that circle — narrowing by circle and `draft` status, because `proposal list` offers no tension filter.

It assembles the change set as a JSON array. Each element needs a non-empty `type`; above that floor the array passes through verbatim. The path does not interpret your change types.

Then the moment this step exists to show you:

```console
$ glassfrog proposal create ten_0123 --changes '[{"type":"MoveAccountability", ...}]'
```

**The write-safety gate interposes and you are asked to confirm.** You see the exact command with the payload **inline** — that is deliberate. A file path or stdin would make you confirm blind, so the change set always rides on the command line where you can read it.

Confirm, and you get a draft record with `action: created`, a `prp_` id, `status: draft`, and a `handoff` id.

Decline, and `action: declined` — nothing was created. That is an outcome, not an error.

This path stops here. It never advances what it drafted.

---

## Step 5 — Advance it into circulation

Take the `prp_` id forward again.

> "Advance prp_0789 into circulation."

`proposal-circulation` delegates to the `proposal-circulator`, which grounds on `proposal get` — reading the proposal exactly as the server returns it — and then runs the transition:

```console
$ glassfrog proposal propose prp_0789
```

**The gate interposes again**, and this is worth pausing on: this is a *second* confirmation, entirely separate from the one in Step 4. Each gated write confirms independently. Nothing is batched or pre-authorized. If you later withdraw this proposal, you will cross the gate a third time.

On success the server returns the proposal in `proposed_outside_meeting`, carrying the **server-set** `response_deadline` and your own implicit `no_objection` in the `response_summary`.

Ask where it stands and you get a monitoring picture — `response_summary`, `response_deadline`, `available_transitions` — read straight from the server, with no write. The path **computes no acceptance**: the proposal's `status` is the signal.

Treat `available_transitions` as narration, not a precondition. The transition is always issued and the server authorizes it; a `422` refusal comes back plainly rather than being guessed at locally.

If the proposal needs amending, withdraw it — the record comes back in `draft` with the deadline cleared and a `handoff` id pointing back to Step 4.

---

## Step 6 — Review a proposal as the responder, and answer it

Now change seats. Someone else's proposal is circulating and it awaits your consent.

> "What proposals are pending on me?"

`proposal-impact-review` loads. Without an id, the reviewer walks `proposal list` in full and returns the circulating proposals awaiting you. Pick one:

> "What would prp_0456 change for my roles?"

The `proposal-impact-reviewer` grounds the proposal, draws your **footprint** (`me`, `me roles`, `me actions`, `me projects`), and reads back the affected governance where the change set touches that footprint. What returns:

- **changes** — the change set drawn out, reflected from the record and never re-interpreted
- **footprint** — your roles, actions, and projects, each with its id
- **footprint_coverage** — **tri-state**: `complete`, `incomplete`, or `unknown`
- **intersections** — where the change lands on you, with current-vs-proposed read-backs

Read the coverage qualifier **before** you trust an empty `intersections`. An empty array is the honest no-impact case — but on `incomplete` or `unknown` it means *not in the roles visible to this read*, not *no impact*.

Now the most important property of this path: **the picture contains no recommended response and no objection ruling.** There is no verdict field for one to hide in. "No objections found" is not an instruction to answer `no_objection`.

You decide. Three outcomes, all first-class — `no_objection`, `bring_to_meeting`, or *not yet*, which leaves the picture as the result and records nothing.

Say what you chose, and the skill records it:

```console
$ glassfrog proposal respond prp_0456 --response no_objection
```

The gate interposes once more. Note where this write runs: **in your context, not the subagent's.** The reviewer has no respond mode at all — if you ask it to record the answer, it refuses by name. Your decision splits the workflow at the read/write seam, and an isolated subagent cannot ask you to decide.

On success you get the recorded response — a `prr_` id, the value, and the parent proposal's status. If that status is `accepted`, your response completed the expected set and closed the consent window. That is surfaced from the record, never computed locally.

---

## What you've learned

You took one concern through all six paths and watched the handoffs: a concern became a picture, an action became a characterization, a tension became a `ten_` id, that id became a `prp_` draft, that draft entered circulation, and a circulating proposal became a recorded `prr_` response.

Along the way you saw the properties that make the surface trustworthy:

- **Every path composes commands the CLI already exposes.** None adds a capability, a command, or a flag.
- **Reading happens in an isolated subagent** and only the synthesized result reaches you — raw output never floods your context.
- **Each path stops at its boundary** and hands off by id rather than continuing into the next job.
- **Governance writes are gated individually.** Tension writes are not — they are operational edits by design.
- **Uncertainty is reported, never smoothed over.** Tri-state ownership and coverage fields exist so an incomplete read never becomes a confident negative.
- **Nothing is fabricated.** A failed read is named and the result built from what succeeded; a rejected write yields no invented id.
